Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

In academic institution s, reading is not a single activity but a family of strategies that learners deploy depending on purpose. When a student needs a general impression of a chapter before deciding whether it is relevant, skimming is appropriate: the reader moves quickly through headings, topic sentences, and summaries to grasp the overall structure and main idea. When the task is to locate a specific fact, date, name, or figure, scanning is more efficient: the eyes search the text selectively for the target information without reading every word. Intensive reading, by contrast, is slow and deliberate; it is used when the material must be understood in detail, evaluated critically, and remembered. Extensive reading involves large quantities of text read for pleasure, fluency, or general knowledge, with less attention to minute detail.

Critical reading goes beyond literal comprehension. A critical reader identifies the author's purpose, distinguishes claims from evidence, notices assumptions, and judges whether the reasoning is sound. This is especially important when synthesizing multiple sources: two authors may describe the same phenomenon but interpret it differently, and the reader must compare their evidence and conclusions rather than merely summarise each in turn. Note-making supports this process. Effective notes are selective, structured, and paraphrased; they record the main ideas and the relationships among them, not a verbatim copy of the text. Tables, graphs, and charts are also texts that must be read and transcoded: a reader should be able to state in words what a table shows, identify trends in a line graph, and explain what a bar chart compares. Information literacy extends these skills to the library and the internet, where the reader must evaluate the credibility, currency, and relevance of sources before using them.

(a) Suggest a suitable title for the passage. **(2 marks)**
(b) State the reading technique most appropriate for each of the following purposes: **(3 marks)**
 

(i) obtaining a general impression of a chapter before deciding whether to read it; **(1 mark)**
(ii) locating a specific date or figure in a text; **(1 mark)**
(iii) understanding and critically evaluating a difficult argument in detail. **(1 mark)**
(c) Identify the metaphor in the first sentence of the passage and explain what it means in not more than one line. **(3 marks)**
(d) According to the passage, critical reading involves several distinct capabilities. List four of them. **(4 marks)**
(e) The passage claims that extensive reading involves less attention to minute detail than intensive reading. True or false? Support your answer with evidence from the passage. **(3 marks)**
(f) In what three ways does note-making support the reading process, according to the passage? **(3 marks)**
(g) How does the passage suggest a reader should handle two sources that interpret the same phenomenon differently? **(3 marks)**
(h) Use one word from the passage that accurately describes notes that are not a verbatim copy of the text. **(2 marks)**
(i) Provide evidence from the passage that the author expects readers to evaluate internet sources before using them. **(2 marks)**

1. Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

The role of theory in explaining complex phenomena in the workplace is widely acknowledged. However, the mere existence of a theory does not always help us understand the realities we face daily. In attempting to understand human actions and behaviour, many psychologists and professionals from related fields often rely on motivational theories. Many earlier theories are well known, but they have not withstood close scrutiny. Nevertheless, there are contemporary theories that share a common feature: each is supported by a reasonable degree of valid documentation. This does not imply that newer theories are unquestionably correct. They are termed contemporary not because they were developed recently but because they provide vital support in explaining employee motivation.

Maslow's needs hierarchy theory has been reworked by Clayton Alderfer in an academic institution, who cites the need to consider new empirical research. His ERG theory argues that human behaviour is driven not by five needs but by three core groups: existence, relatedness, and growth. The existence group concerns basic material requirements, including what Maslow called physiological and safety needs. The second category involves the need to establish and maintain important interpersonal relationships. Social and status desires require interaction with others and align with Maslow's social need. The ERG theory isolates growth need, an intrinsic desire for personal development, which corresponds to Maslow's esteem and self-actualization needs.

In addition to reducing five needs to three, Alderfer argues that more than one need may operate simultaneously and that if gratification of a higher need is stifled, the desire to satisfy a lower need increases. Maslow's hierarchy is rigid and assumes step-like progression. ERG does not assume a rigid hierarchy in which a lower need must be substantially gratified before moving on. For instance, a person can work on growth even when existence and relatedness needs are unsatisfied, or all three need categories may operate at once.

Alderfer's extrapolation is seen as frustrating because, unlike Maslow's case where an individual gets stuck and makes more effort to meet an unmet higher need, in ERG the individual compensates for the lack of attainment of a higher need with more effort in meeting lower level needs. This contemporary theory is more consistent with what we know about individual differences, as variables such as family background, education, and cultural environment alter the importance or driving force that a group of needs holds for a particular individual.

READING COMPREHENSION **

**READ THIS PASSAGE AND ANSWER THE QUESTIONS WHICH FOLLOW IT**

The world has witnessed extensive national, regional and global conservation activities all aimed at both protecting and conserving the sanctity of our environment. Sensitization campaigns as multiplicity of practical interventions have enjoyed millions of dollars all in an attempt to avert the very inevitability of severely damaged ecosystem. In spite of the numerous environmental protection efforts that have been initiated, problems emanating from environmental degradation are increasingly becoming more lethal and stand of threaten our very existence as humans. The combined effects global warming, deforestation, air and water pollution bear upon us only one inevitable consequence. We have no environmental legacy. We have only but trouble to bequeath the generations of the future. The current burden of human suffering resulting from a lost environmental equilibrium is too much to bear. Extreme drought, famine, server flooding, loss of biodiversity and rising poverty levels are major threat to our common existence.

Is it too hard one wonders to conserve the environment even with the colossal gains in view that would accrue from our collective efforts? Conserving the environment is not at all easy. Even if we had all the fiscal resources at our disposal, we still would fall short in our efforts. The polarity of views as to what constitutes effective conservation measures would be the first barrier to stare us in the face. Even if we agree on that one, other hurdles would be presented by human greed for selfish economic gain, poverty, cultural differences and social and environmental injustice issues.

Environmental pollution as a human quandary traces its very birth to human economic development with particular reference to the industrial revolution. Even though this phase of

{*INVOLVEMENT IN EXAMINATION IRREGULARITY WILL LEAD TO...*}

Paradoxically, even the industrial nations themselves have to contend with the byp0roduct of their wealth creation. They breath unclean air, are facing the dangers of extreme climatic conditions and they die in their millions for the aftermath of consumerism.

The nexus between social-economic political systems and environmental quality is also worth some degree of attention. Environmental safety is strongly linked to the institution al character of every nation. Countries that are defined by inclusiveness would be assumed to fare better in their conservation efforts as opposed to countries defined by extractive industry. The former tend to level the ground for all and hence have strong laws to protect environmental resources from exploitation by a few for their own selfish economic gain. But even in these countries, pollution runs rampant. Extractive nations misuse political power in allowing only a minority to extract resources from the many in the pursuit of selfish gain. The latter will be the case in poor nations.
